assumptions.text: One stream-aligned team of two part-time developers (manifest teams=1, C2); named 'library team'. No platform or enabling team exists.
The website is served by the same deployable (server-rendered pages); no separately released frontend bundle is evidenced, so none is listed.

One deployable. Until D1 is closed the artifact builds option A: the five clock commands run on an in-process scheduler that calls the same entrypoints a human can call with an as-of date; each run takes a Postgres advisory lock and writes a job_run row.

Missed runs must be visible without on-call: C2 forbids babysitting and strategize B1 measures on-time share after three months, which is only evidence if the reminder job provably ran. A job_run row is required under every option.

open_questions.text: Where will the app be hosted, and does that host offer a cron/scheduled-task facility (which would make option C free) or force a second process for scheduled work?
Who would notice that a night's jobs did not run, and is a last-run line on the coordinator's screen enough, or is an emailed nightly summary needed?

notes_for_downstream.text: Decision D1 (who fires the clock commands) is open pending Q1; the default built is A. Code: every clock command is a driving port that takes asOfDate, can be called by hand, holds a Postgres advisory lock and writes a job_run row - with no assumption about who calls it (in-process scheduler, a worker, or a host cron), so any option can be taken at deploy time without touching the domain.

expire-reservations and lapse-memberships have no entry in connect messages[]; they appear only in connect N1 prose. Three of five clock commands carry payload, delivery and idempotency; connect should add the other two on a re-run so define and contracts see them.

Supersedes the operative reading of connect N2: its outbox condition is a split by context. Organise splits by neither; the clock commands span three contexts, so even a same-code worker keeps loan-overdue and item-returned in-process. Do not re-run connect on this decision.

teams.name: Library team
teams.notes: Two part-time developers, no on-call (C2). Four modules in one deployable, one external integration (Stripe) plus email: within the rubric for a small team.

deployables.name: Toolshare app
deployables.rationale: One team, one Postgres (C3), every cross-context hop in-process (connect); no runtime, scaling, regulatory or stack reason in the inputs to split any module. The clock commands run inside it on an in-process scheduler until D1 says otherwise.

scale_check.note: 1 of a 1-3 target. Why not fewer: one is the minimum. Why not more: the only candidate is a same-code worker for the five clock commands (decision D1, open on Q1) - a second process for two part-time developers that buys starvation and double-run protection an advisory lock already gives; a same-code worker keeps loan-overdue and item-returned in-process (connect N2's outbox condition is a split by context, which no option does). inventory and lending are async-only inbound and cheap to extract later, but nothing in the inputs asks for it.

plain_words.what: We decided who owns which part and how many separate programs get deployed.
plain_words.decided: One team of two owns all four parts. One program to deploy, holding all four modules and one database.
plain_words.assumed: That the nightly jobs (late fees, reminders, expiring holds) can run inside the same program on a timer, as long as every run is recorded and locked - who pulls the trigger (timer in the app or the host's cron) is left open until the host is known (D1).
plain_words.riskiest: If a night's jobs silently do not run and nobody built the run log, late fees stop accruing and reminders stop going out, and the 90% target cannot even be measured.

decisions.question: Who fires the five clock-driven commands - an in-process scheduler, a same-code worker deployable, or the host's cron - and how is a missed run noticed?

options.summary: One modular monolith; a scheduler library in the app fires the five clock commands, each an entrypoint taking asOfDate, callable by hand, holding an advisory lock and writing a job_run row.
pros: One deploy, one process, one log (C2, C3)
No process boundary, so connect's in-memory events stay valid
cons: A job that silently does not fire is invisible without monitoring
Two app instances would double-run jobs unless locked
risks: Late fees quietly stop accruing after a restart and nobody notices for weeks (G2)

options.summary: The monolith plus a separate scheduled worker deployable running the clock commands from the same code.
pros: Jobs cannot be starved by web traffic and cannot double-run with a single worker
Worker failures are a visible, separate signal
cons: A second process to deploy and watch for two part-time developers

A second runtime to keep in version step; it buys starvation and double-run protection that an advisory lock and the existing idempotency keys already give (a same-code worker keeps loan-overdue and item-returned in-process)
risks: Distributed failure modes arrive before the library has any scale

options.summary: One monolith; the host's scheduled task invokes the same job entrypoints (app run-job <name> --as-of); no scheduler code in the repo.
pros: No scheduler code and no second process; the host reports missed runs
cons: Depends on the host offering cron (Q1)
Job endpoints must be protected and idempotent
risks: A host migration silently loses the schedule

would_flip_if: the host offers a scheduled-task facility that alerts on a failed or missed run (take C)
the web app will run more than one instance, counting rolling deploys (advisory lock becomes mandatory; A loses its simplicity edge over C)
nobody would notice a missed night until the annual audit (a job_run row is not enough; an emailed nightly summary is a separate piece of work)
decisions.rationale: OPEN. Strategist recommendation: A, sharpened with three riders (asOfDate entrypoints, job_run row, advisory lock); C is a genuine upgrade if and only if Q1 says the host offers a scheduled-task facility that reports a failed or missed run, and A and C share one codebase so the switch is a deploy-time change. Left without `chosen` because the human who knows the host must make that call; the artifact builds A meanwhile (A2).
